As for 'the armies of the heavens and the earth', al-Tabari sees them as helpers through whom God takes vengeance on enemies, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Abbas list angels, jinn and humans, and al-Razi also includes heavenly and earthly causes. The commentators conclude that God knows His creatures and is wise in His governance, and that this tranquility prepared the believers for victory and reward.

This verse states that God sent tranquillity into the hearts of the believers and granted this victory, so that He would admit the believing men and women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, to remain in them forever, and would remove their evil deeds; this, the verse says, is a great triumph in God's sight. Most commentators connect the purpose of admission to what precedes it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi link it to the success of Hudaybiyya or to the increase of faith, while al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur link it rather to the divine arrangement and trial involving the armies of the heavens and the earth. All agree that this triumph means deliverance from every distress and attainment of every desired good. They also explain that mentioning admission before the expiation of sins does not follow the order of events but gives priority to the highest aim, as Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi note. Al-Baghawi, al-Tabari and others report the occasion of revelation: after the verse about the Prophet's forgiveness, the companions said it was good news for him and asked what would be given to them. On the expiation of sins, Ibn Kathir understands it as pardon and covering, and al-Sha'rawi explains that God conceals them so they do not spoil the believers' bliss. Finally, the explicit mention of believing women, according to al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur, prevents the reading that the reward concerns only men.

This passage of Surat al-Fath describes the fate of hypocrite men and women and polytheist men and women who harbored a bad opinion of God, thinking that He would not support His Messenger ﷺ and the believers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that they believed God would not grant victory to Muhammad and the believers or let His word prevail, and that the evil turn would fall back on them as humiliation and punishment. Al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari read the 'circle of evil' as the scheme they plotted against the Muslims, which ends up striking them. Al-Baghawi specifies that the hypocrites were in Medina and the polytheists in Mecca. Ibn al-Jawzi lists several views on this bad opinion, including the belief that God would not raise the dead or that He has a partner, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that all their false opinions about God are meant. The commentators agree that divine anger, curse, expulsion from mercy and Hell are their punishment. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir connect the verse to the context of Hudaybiyya, when the truce had saddened some believers before it proved to be a clear victory. The readings differ on 'dā'irat al-sū' ': the fatha reading is the common one, while Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a damma. Grammarians note that the two forms are close in meaning, the first being more usual when a blameworthy noun is attached. Ibn al-Qayyim sees polytheism as the gravest form of bad thinking about God, and al-Sha'rawi includes denying His existence, His attributes or the resurrection under the same heading.

This part of the verse states that the armies of the heavens and the earth belong to God alone, and that God is mighty and wise. Commentators connect it to the preceding verses about the punishment of hypocrites and polytheists who thought God would not support the Prophet after the treaty of Hudaybiyya. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri explain that God can help His Prophet and religion without the believers, since He controls all forces. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi also read a warning in it: these armies are those of punishment, which explains why the name "Mighty" is used rather than "Knowing". Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur stress this point, and al-Qasimi reports that al-Qashani sees in it a reminder of the superiority of earthly forces over the hypocrites. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi relate that Ibn Abbas understood these armies to be the angels and the believers, while al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari also mention the tranquillity granted to believers and the punishment of disbelievers. Al-Qurtubi notes that some included all creatures. Readers differ on the word "su'": the Kufans and al-Farra' read it with a fatha, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr with a damma. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the fatha form refers to what is blamed, and the damma form to what is harmful. Ibn Ashur adds that "mighty" means that no conqueror can overcome God.

This verse states that God sent the Prophet ﷺ as a witness over his community, a bearer of good news of Paradise to those who obey him, and a warner of punishment to those who disobey. Commentators read the witness in two ways: Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it as witness to the delivery of the message, while al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi also include witness over people's deeds, good or bad. Al-Razi links it to testifying to God's oneness. Readers differ on the verbs that follow, reading them either in the second person plural ("that you may believe") or the third person plural; al-Tabari holds both readings to be correct. On the meaning of "ta'zir", al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and Ibn 'Abbas explain it as honouring and exalting, Qatada and Ikrima as supporting and fighting alongside him, and Ibn Zayd as obedience. On the pronouns, most commentators, including Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Sa'di, refer them to the Prophet, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi refer them to God. Glorifying God (tasbih) is understood by some as declaring Him free of every flaw, and by others as the prayers, with Ibn 'Abbas specifying the dawn and afternoon prayers. These words are also linked to the pledge at al-Hudaybiyya: Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that those who pledged were in truth pledging to God. As for the content of the pledge, Salama ibn al-Akwa' reports it was to face death, while Jabir reports it was not to flee.

This verse states the purpose of the Prophet's mission as witness, bringer of good news and warner: that people believe in God and His Messenger, that they support and honour the Messenger, and that they glorify God morning and evening. Readers differ on the four imperative verbs: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read them in the third person, while most read them in the second person; al-Tabari considers both readings valid and equivalent in meaning. The commentators agree that ta'zir means to honour and support, and tawqir means to revere and magnify; Qatada and Ikrima understand support as fighting with the sword, while Ibn Zayd understands it as obedience. On the pronouns, the majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, refer the first two verbs to the Prophet and the tasbih to God; al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi refer them all to God, and al-Razi prefers that view. As for tasbih, Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean the dawn, midday and afternoon prayers, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi speak of prayer generally, while Ibn 'Ashur sees morning and evening as an expression for the whole day.

This verse states that the pledge the believers made to the Prophet ﷺ at Hudaybiyya, known as the Pledge of Good Pleasure, is in reality a pledge to God, since obeying the Messenger is obeying God and it is God who promises Paradise to those who keep their word. Commentators report that the participants pledged not to flee from the enemy: according to Salama ibn al-Akwa' they swore to die, while Jabir ibn 'Abdullah says they swore only not to flee. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi also report that no one broke the oath except al-Jadd ibn Qays, who hid under his camel. As for the phrase "the hand of God is above their hands", al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi give two readings: God's hand is above their loyalty and reward, or God's strength and support are above their own strength and support. Al-Kalbi understands it as God's favour in guidance, Ibn Kaysan as divine power, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi see it as an image meant to reinforce the bond of allegiance to the Messenger, without attributing organs to God. Ibn Kathir keeps a more literal reading while affirming God's transcendence, and Ibn Sa'di sees it as emphasis on the firmness of the covenant. All agree that whoever breaks the pledge harms only himself and whoever keeps it will receive a great reward, Paradise, with the readings differing only in the verb form for "He will give him".

In this verse God tells His Prophet what the Bedouins who stayed behind from the Hudaybiyya 'umra will say: they will claim that their goods and families kept them busy and will ask him to seek forgiveness for them. God refutes their claim, since their tongues say what is not in their hearts. He then tells the Prophet to ask them who could secure anything for them against God if He willed harm or benefit, the implied answer being no one, and that God is fully aware of what they do. The commentators agree that these were the tribes of Ghifar, Muzayna, Juhayna, Ashja', Aslam and Dil, who stayed back out of fear of Quraysh, supposing that the Prophet and his companions would never return. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi hold that their request for forgiveness was not accompanied by repentance and was a matter of outward appeasement. Ibn 'Abbas said that doubt was in their hearts, and al-Razi analyses the structure of their excuse in detail, seeing it as an attempt to conceal their real motive. Ibn 'Ashur notes that some of them were not hypocrites, though their faith had not fully taken root. On recitation, al-Tabari prefers the reading of 'darran' with a fatha, since it is paired with 'naf'an', while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma. Ibn Kathir and others see in the passage both a warning about the fate of those who hold back and a reminder that all power belongs to God alone.

This verse exposes the real reason some Bedouins stayed behind from the Prophet ﷺ during the Hudaybiyya expedition. They had claimed that their possessions and families kept them busy and asked him to seek forgiveness for them, but God reveals what they concealed: they thought the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, and Satan made this thought seem attractive in their hearts. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain that their excuse was a pretext and flattery rather than sincere repentance. The commentators differ on the word "bur": Mujahid and Ibn Abbas take it to mean "ruined" or "perished", while Qatada and Ibn Zayd understand it as "corrupt" or "lacking all good", and al-Tabari notes that it is a word from the dialect of Oman. Al-Zamakhshari suggests they were corrupt in their souls and intentions, or doomed in God's sight and deserving of His wrath. As for the "evil thought", al-Razi considers that it may be the belief that God would break His promise or that the Messenger was lying, whereas the majority take it as their conviction that God would not support His Prophet. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir stress that the closing part of the passage reminds us that God forgives whoever repents and punishes those who persist in disbelief. The commentators thus agree on the core message: a stern warning against thinking ill of God.

This part of the verse declares that whoever does not combine faith in Allah with faith in His Messenger is a disbeliever, and that Allah has prepared for him a blazing fire. Most commentators read the verse as addressing the Bedouins who stayed behind from the Prophet at Hudaybiyya, whose bad opinion of Allah and His Messenger has just been rebuked. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud agree that it is a threat against unbelievers. They explain that using the phrase "the disbelievers" instead of a pronoun shows that anyone who does not combine the two faiths is a disbeliever. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi note that the indefinite form "sa'ir" serves to inspire awe or refers to a specific kind of fire. Ibn 'Abbas, quoted by Ibn Kathir, says the sa'ir is the sixth level of Hell. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the threat is mixed with some respite and hope, since these people had not openly rejected faith and Allah knew they would believe. Al-Tabari takes the people addressed to be hypocrites among the Bedouins, and al-Qurtubi says that their hypocrisy amounts to disbelief. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur link the phrase to a warning against doubt that could lead from faith to disbelief. The general meaning is therefore shared: refusing both faiths leads to punishment, and the next phrase reminds the reader that dominion belongs to Allah, who forgives and punishes as He wills.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the warning to the Bedouins who stayed behind and did not join the Prophet at Hudaybiyya, and that its plain meaning is that God alone owns the heavens and the earth, forgives whom He wills, punishes whom He wills, and is Forgiving and Merciful. Al-Tabari reads it as an exhortation to those Bedouins to repent and return to obedience to the Messenger, since God forgives the repentant. Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di share this reading: God's will is exercised with wisdom, forgiving the sincere believer and punishing the unbeliever or the persistent hypocrite, and His mercy precedes His wrath. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan hold that God's will follows His wisdom, which requires forgiving the penitent and punishing the one who persists, and Zamakhshari adds that minor sins are expiated by avoiding major ones while major sins are forgiven through repentance; Abu Hayyan notes that this view reflects Mu'tazilite doctrine. Al-Razi says that mentioning God's sovereignty affirms the greatness of both reward and punishment. Al-Tha'alibi and Ibn 'Ashur see the verse as holding out hope of forgiveness to these men, with the phrase "whom He wills" covering causes and conditions that the Qur'an and Sunna detail elsewhere. Al-Qurtubi notes that God needs none of His creatures and that He imposes duties in order to reward good and punish evil.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that those left behind from the Hudaybiyya expedition will ask to follow him when he sets out for the spoils of Khaybar, saying: let us follow you. The commentators explain that this request aims to change God's promise to the people of Hudaybiyya, that the spoils of Khaybar would be theirs alone as compensation for what they had missed at Mecca. God therefore tells him to reply that they will not follow him, as God said this beforehand. They will then claim that the refusal stems from envy of them, and God answers that they understand little. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the words of God refer to this promise, while Ibn Zayd takes them to refer to the command in the Tawba verse (83) not to go out with the Prophet. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir reject this view, since the Tawba verse was revealed after the Tabuk campaign, years later. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the plural form "kalim", with a similar meaning. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Biqa'i and Ibn Ashur read the two uses of "bal" differently: the first rejects the claim that the prohibition comes from God, while the second moves the hypocrites from the charge of envy to a graver fault, ignorance and poor understanding. Ibn Ashur explains that envy here means eagerness to keep the spoils for oneself. Most commentators identify the spoils as those of Khaybar, which they consider the closest in context.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say to the desert Arabs who stayed behind that they will be called later to fight a people of great might, and that they must either fight them or the people will submit. Obeying that call brings a good reward, while turning away as they did at Hudaybiyya brings a painful punishment. The commentators differ widely on who these people are. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, Ibn Abi Layla and 'Ata' al-Khurasani say they are the Persians, Ka'b says the Byzantines, al-Hasan says both Persians and Byzantines, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima and Qatada say the Hawazin and Thaqif at the battle of Hunayn, al-Zuhri and Muqatil say the Banu Hanifa followers of Musaylima, and Abu Hurayra says they have not yet come. Al-Tabari declines to fix a specific group, finding no decisive evidence, while Ibn Kathir leans toward the Banu Hanifa on the authority of Rafi' ibn Khadij. Most agree on the general sense: a people who accept only Islam or the sword, according to some, while others allow the jizya from Magians and People of the Book. Some scholars, including al-Razi, cite the verse in support of the caliphates of Abu Bakr and Umar, a claim others dispute. Ubayy's reading, « aw yuslimu », is reported with the sense of « until they submit ». The verse is followed by the exemption of the blind, the lame and the sick from blame.

This verse states that the blind, the lame and the sick bear no blame for staying away from fighting, since their condition prevents them. It adds that whoever obeys God and His Messenger will be admitted into gardens with rivers flowing beneath them, while whoever turns away will receive a painful punishment. The commentators report that it was revealed after the people of excuses, frightened by the threat against those who stayed behind, asked what would become of them. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak take the exemption to concern jihad, the stated infirmities preventing advance and retreat. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that this ruling applies to every campaign until the Day of Resurrection, and that a disabled person who joins anyway receives a doubled reward; he cites Ibn Umm Maktum, who was blind and carried the standard at al-Qadisiyya. Al-Razi analyses which disabilities qualify, and notes that the loss of both hands is not mentioned because it is rare.

The main disagreement concerns the people "of great might" to whom the absent will be summoned. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Mujahid say they are the Persians, Ka'b and al-Hasan the Romans, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada the Hawazin at Hunayn, al-Zuhri and Muqatil the Banu Hanifa followers of Musaylima, while Abu Hurayra says they have not yet come. Al-Shawkani and Ibn Sa'di favour a general reading, and al-Alusi treats these identifications as examples. On recitation, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read the two verbs in the first person plural, whereas most readers use the third person; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer the latter.

This verse states that God was pleased with the believers who pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ under the tree at Hudaybiyya. He knew what was in their hearts, sent down tranquility upon them, and granted them a near victory. The commentators agree on the occasion: word spread that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, sent to the Quraysh, had been killed, so the Prophet called the people to pledge to fight. They differ on the content of the pledge. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said they swore not to flee, not to die, while others reported that it was a pledge unto death. Muqatil took 'what was in their hearts' to mean reluctance to pledge unto death, a view Ibn 'Atiyya considered demeaning to the Companions. Estimates of the number present range from about thirteen hundred to fifteen hundred and twenty-five, and the figure of fourteen hundred is the most favoured. Most say the near victory is the conquest of Khaybar, while some say it is Mecca. Several report that 'Umar had the tree cut down to prevent people venerating it. The commentators conclude that the verse honours those who took this pledge.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the Pledge of Good Pleasure under the tree at Hudaybiyya. God declared His pleasure with the believers who pledged to the Prophet ﷺ to stand firm and not to flee. He knew the sincerity of their hearts, sent down tranquillity upon them, rewarded them with a near victory and promised them abundant spoils. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi hold that the near victory and these spoils refer to the conquest of Khaybar and its wealth, reserved for those who gave the pledge. Qatada and al-Hasan suggested it could mean the conquest of Mecca or other conquests, while Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi understood the many spoils as every booty the Muslims would take until the Day of Resurrection. Opinions differ on the number who pledged: Jabir reports fourteen hundred, Ibn Abbas one thousand five hundred and twenty-five, and Ibn Abi Awfa one thousand three hundred. On the nature of the pledge, some reports say it was a pledge unto death, whereas Jabir insisted it was only a pledge not to flee. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir emphasise that God's might and wisdom appear in the fulfilment of these promises.

The commentators explain that God promised the believers who took part in Hudaybiyya many spoils, and that He hastened for them this immediate gain and restrained from them the hands of those who meant them harm. On what this hastened spoil is, at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi identify it as the spoils of Khaybar, Mujahid links it to all conquests, while Ibn Abbas, in al-Awfi's report, takes it to be the Hudaybiyya treaty itself. The many spoils promised are, for Mujahid, al-Nasafi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, everything the Muslims will take until the Day of Resurrection, and for al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Layla, the lands of Persia and Byzantium. As for the restrained hands, Qatada, at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir name the Jews who planned to raid the families left in Medina, al-Muqatil names the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan who came to support Khaybar and were struck with terror, and Ibn Abbas and others name the Meccans bound by the treaty. At-Tabari, relying on the following verse, rules out the Meccans here. The phrase 'a sign for the believers' is read either as that very restraint, or as proof that Khaybar confirms the promise of conquering Mecca. The 'straight path' is for most the trust and reliance upon God, and for others an increase in insight and certainty.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the passage on the spoils God promised the believers, and that the 'other' refers to a gain or conquest the Muslims could not yet obtain at the time, but which God has encompassed in His knowledge and power, so that it will be theirs. They differ on its identity. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Muqatil and Ibn Abi Layla take it to be the lands of Persia and Byzantium and whatever else the Muslims would conquer. Al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq say it is Khaybar, while Qatada says it is Makkah, a view al-Tabari prefers because the verse addresses those of the Pledge of Ridwan who had tried to reach Makkah and failed. Mujahid takes it as every spoil until the Day of Resurrection, and 'Ikrima as the spoils of Hunayn. Most read 'God has encompassed it' as meaning mastery and control, while others mean protection or foreknowledge that it will be theirs. Al-Zamakhshari offers an unusual grammatical reading that Abu Hayyan considers odd. The verse closes by affirming God's power over all things, which the commentators note fits every one of these readings.

This verse tells the believers that if the disbelievers had fought them, they would have turned their backs in flight and found neither protector nor helper. It describes a fixed custom of God that never changes. The commentators agree that the verse brings reassurance to the believers at the time of Hudaybiyya and affirms that God consistently supports His messengers and friends. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Qurtubi identify the disbelievers as the Quraysh of Mecca, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi allow that they could be the allies of the people of Khaybar, and Ibn Atiyya reports that the custom may refer to the battle of Badr.

On the meaning of the word sunna, al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya explain that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning that God established this as a rule. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di read it as the general principle that truth prevails when belief and disbelief meet, with Badr as an example. Al-Razi holds that this victory is decreed by God and not a matter of chance or of the influence of the stars. Ibn al-Qayyim treats it as a promise conditional on patience and piety, which explains the setback at Uhud. Ibn Ashur argues that the completeness of victory depends on the faith and steadfastness of the army, and al-Jaza'iri takes it as a rule valid in every time and place.

The commentators explain that this verse (48:23) affirms that God has established a constant practice, as with earlier peoples, of granting victory to His allies over their enemies, and that this practice cannot be changed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that if the disbelievers fought the believers they would turn and flee, finding neither protector nor helper, and that the word sunna is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun, meaning that God instituted this practice. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it as the victory of the prophets and their followers, citing the verse 'I and My messengers will surely prevail.' Al-Razi distinguishes this divine practice from the claim of astrologers that the rising sign decides victory: God is a free agent who does not change His custom. Ibn al-Qayyim links the promise to the condition of patience and piety, a condition that was not met at Uhud because of the companions' cowardice and disobedience. Ibn 'Ashur adds that victory may be complete in danger and alternating in ease, and depends on adherence to the Prophet's instructions. The exegetes agree on the message of encouragement to the believers but differ on who the disbelievers are: Quraysh according to most, or Asad, Ghatafan and the people of Khaybar, or the Byzantines and Persians. Few of them draw any legal ruling from this verse.

This verse recalls God's favour to the believers: it was He who restrained the hands of the unbelievers from you and your hands from them in the 'valley of Makkah', that is at Hudaybiyya near the sanctuary, after He had given you the upper hand over them. Most commentators agree that the occasion was a group of around eighty men from Makkah who came down from the Tan'im hills armed, intending to surprise the Prophet and his companions at dawn. They were taken captive and then pardoned and released, as narrated by Anas ibn Malik, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, and 'Abdullah ibn Mughaffal gives a similar account by the tree of Hudaybiyya. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Juzayy and others see this episode as one of the reasons behind the truce.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also cite the report of Ibn Abza, in which Khalid ibn al-Walid drove back Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl's force as far as the walls of Makkah, though Ibn Kathir considers this chronology doubtful, since Khalid had not yet embraced Islam at Hudaybiyya. Ibn Ishaq and Qurtubi report that the Quraysh showered the camp with stones and arrows. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi record other views on who the restrained hands were: the Jews of Madina, the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan who came to aid Khaybar, or Quraysh.

On the meaning of 'the valley of Makkah', Al-Razi, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan take it either as Makkah itself or as Hudaybiyya, which is partly within the sanctuary. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the phrase may mean the centre of the city, but he finds that the events it refers to occurred at Hudaybiyya. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hanifa take the verse to imply that Makkah was conquered by force, a reading others reject, and Al-Qasimi and Ibn Kathir stress that the victory here was the capture of the men. On recitation, Abu 'Amr reads 'ya'malun' in the third person as a warning to the unbelievers, while the others read 'ta'malun' in the second person; in both cases God sees what each side does.

This passage of Surah al-Fath recalls that the disbelievers of Mecca, who rejected the oneness of God, barred the believers from the Sacred Mosque and held back the sacrificial animals (hady) so that they could not reach their place of sacrifice, the Haram. The commentators explain that fighting would have been ordered had it not been for believing men and women living among the Meccans who concealed their faith and could be killed by mistake, bringing a blame called ma'arra upon the Muslims. The scholars differ on its meaning: Ibn Zayd takes it as sin, Ibn Ishaq as the blood-money, and al-Tabari as expiation, while others understand it as the reproach of the unbelievers or as inner distress. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir consider the first two views weak for killing a believer whose faith is hidden among enemies, and the commentators do not decide between them. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the answer to the condition is implied, and that God restrained the Muslims out of mercy for the weak believers and so that some Meccans might enter Islam after the truce. Ibn Kathir adds that this restraint was also the reason the conquest was delayed. As for ''lo tazayyalu'', most read it as: if they had separated and been distinguished from the unbelievers, the unbelievers would have been punished by the sword at the hands of the Muslims. The passage also recalls, according to most commentators, that the word of piety is 'there is no god but God', and that the believers were most worthy of it.

This verse describes the Quraysh at Hudaybiyya: when those who disbelieved placed in their hearts a zealous pride, the pride of the age of ignorance, they refused to write "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" and to acknowledge the Prophet's mission, and they barred him and his companions from entering the Sacred Mosque that year. God then sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, so they did not answer that pride with anger or fighting. He made them hold to the word of piety. The commentators differ on what this word is. Most, including Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, say it is "There is no god but God"; 'Ata al-Khurasani adds "Muhammad is the Messenger of God"; 'Ata Ibn Abi Rabah says "alone, without partner"; al-Zuhri says it is the basmala; and al-Hasan says it is fulfilling the covenant. On the phrase "and they were more worthy of it and fit for it," al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand it as the believers being more deserving than the disbelievers, while al-Razi offers several readings, including the sense of rightfulness without comparison. All agree that God knows everything. Most hold that the treaty of Hudaybiyya was a near victory, while Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak refer it to the conquest of Khaybar.

This verse states that God confirmed the truth of His Messenger's dream, which he had before setting out for Hudaybiyya: in it, he and his companions entered the Sacred Mosque in safety, some shaving their heads and others trimming their hair. The companions expected this to happen that very year. When they were prevented from reaching the House and returned without entering, the hypocrites cast doubt on the dream, so the verse was revealed to affirm that the vision was true and would be fulfilled in its time. Commentators differ on several points. Abu 'Ubayda takes 'in' to mean 'idh' (since), al-Tha'alibi and others report that God made a reservation about what He knows so that people would do the same about what they do not know, al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl suggests that some of those present might die before entering, while others see the exception as a lesson in good manners for believers, or as relating to safety rather than entry. As for 'what you did not know', al-Kalbi explains that the entry would come a year later, al-Tabari and others that there were believers in Mecca unknown to the Muslims who would have been harmed in an assault, while al-Jalalayn sees the wisdom of the treaty. On the 'near victory', most exegetes identify it with the Treaty of Hudaybiyya, Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak with the conquest of Khaybar, and al-Zuhri holds that no conquest in Islam was greater, since it spread the faith. Al-Tabari concludes that both meanings should be included together.

This verse states that Allah sent His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ with guidance, meaning clear proof, and the religion of truth, Islam, so that He might make it prevail over all other religions. The commentators explain this prevailing in closely related ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as the abolition of all other creeds at the descent of Jesus, son of Mary, who will kill the Dajjal, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as superiority through argument and proof, which they see as already visible. All agree that the phrase "Allah suffices as a witness" means that God's testimony guarantees the fulfilment of His promise, or the truth of the prophethood through miracles. The context is the Prophet's vision about entering Mecca, which reassures the believers after the treaty of Hudaybiyya that some had resented. Most identify the "near victory" with the treaty itself, the conquest of Khaybar or the conquest of Mecca, and the vision was fulfilled the following year. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the phrase "if Allah wills" is a lesson in courtesy taught to believers and does not express doubt. All recognise Islam as the true religion, but they differ over the timing and nature of this triumph, and over the exact meaning of guidance and the religion of truth.

This passage of Surat al-Fath describes the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and those with him, as the commentators explain it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the plain sense to be that they are firm and unyielding toward the disbelievers, while showing mercy and affection among themselves, like a father toward his child. The exegetes describe them as constant in bowing and prostrating in prayer, seeking by this God's bounty, His pleasure and Paradise. As for the mark on their faces 'from the trace of prostration', opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan read it as a good bearing, humility and khushu'; Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrima as the trace of dust on the forehead; 'Ata' al-'Awfi, al-Hasan and al-Zuhri as a light and whiteness that will appear on the Day of Resurrection; others as the pallor of night vigils. Al-Razi and al-Tabari consider both the worldly and the otherworldly meanings possible. All agree that this description is found in the Torah. Their image in the Gospel is a seed that sends up its first shoots, grows strong, stands firm on its stalk and delights the sower; most commentators read it as the Prophet, alone at first like the single grain, followed by his companions who multiplied and grew strong. They explain that this growth is meant to enrage the disbelievers, and al-Alusi and al-Qurtubi note that the unbelievers are vexed by the strength of the believers. The verse ends with God's promise to those among them who believed and did righteous deeds of forgiveness and a great reward; al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take 'min' in 'among them' as explaining the kind rather than a part, so the promise covers every believer of that kind.
